1.q: בָּ⁠עֵ֤ת הַ⁠הִיא֙ נְאֻם־יְהוָ֔ה אֶֽהְיֶה֙ לֵֽ⁠אלֹהִ֔ים לְ⁠כֹ֖ל מִשְׁפְּח֣וֹת יִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל וְ⁠הֵ֖מָּה יִֽהְיוּ־לִ֥⁠י לְ⁠עָֽם
1.note: The words that the ULT translates as **At that time** indicate that what Yahweh describes here will happen at the same time as the events that he has just described. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could describe the time relationship more explicitly. Alternate translation: [When those things happen”—the declaration of Yahweh—“I will be for God to all of the clans of Israel, and they will be my people]
See how you translated **the declaration of Yahweh** in 1:8. This also occurs in verses 14, 16, 17, 20, 27, 28, 31–34, and 36–38 of this chapter.

1.q: אֶֽהְיֶה֙ לֵֽ⁠אלֹהִ֔ים לְ⁠כֹ֖ל מִשְׁפְּח֣וֹת יִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל וְ⁠הֵ֖מָּה יִֽהְיוּ־לִ֥⁠י לְ⁠עָֽם
1.note: The implication is that Yahweh is describing a covenant relationship in which he commits himself to the people of Israel and they belong to him. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [I will be the God of all the clans of Israel by covenant, and they will belong to me as my own people]

Yahweh is using **I will be for God** as a common expression of the culture to mean “I will be their God.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I will be their God] or [I will be the one they worship as God]

The pronoun **I** refers to Yahweh, who is speaking about himself through Jeremiah. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [I, Yahweh, will be for God to all of the clans of Israel]

Yahweh is using the possessive form to describe **clans** that belong to the nation of **Israel**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [to all the clans that belong to the nation of Israel]

2.note: See how you translated **Thus says Yahweh** in 2:5. This also occurs in verses 7, 15, 16, 23, 35, and 37 of this chapter.

Here, **the sword** represents warfare and the killing that takes place in it. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the ones who survived the slaughter of battle]

The pronoun **his** refers to **Israel**, that is, to the people of Israel as a group. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [Israel, that is, the people of Israel, going to find their rest]

3.note: The pronoun **me** refers to the people of Israel, to whom Yahweh is speaking through Jeremiah. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [Yahweh appeared to us Israelites]
Here Jeremiah begins to quote the words that Yahweh spoke to his people. Consider natural ways of introducing direct quotations in your language. Alternate translation: [and Yahweh said to me,]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **love**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [And I have loved you forever]

Here Yahweh is speaking as if his **covenant faithfulness** were a cord with which he could draw the people of Israel to himself. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I have brought you to myself by remaining faithful to my covenant]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **covenant faithfulness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [because I am faithful to my covenant with you]
The term translated as **Therefore** indicates that what follows is a result of what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes this clear. Alternate translation: [This is why]

4.note: Here Yahweh is speaking of the people of Israel as if they were a city or a house that he would **build**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Again I will restore you, and you will be restored]

The expression **you will be built** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [I will build you, and I will surely rebuild you]
See how you translated the similar expression in 18:13. This also occurs in verses 4 and 21.

Yahweh is using the possessive form to describe a **dance** that is characterized by the merriment of **the ones laughing**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the dance where people laugh with merriment]

5.note: Yahweh is using the possessive form to describe **mountains** that are in the region of **Samaria**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the mountains that are located in Samaria]

Yahweh is using **will treat them as common** as a common expression of the culture to mean “will freely enjoy the fruit of the vineyards themselves.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the planters will plant and will enjoy the fruit themselves]

6.note: The word translated as **For** indicates that what follows is a reason for what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what came before. Alternate translation: [This is because] This also occurs in verses 7, 9, 11, 16, 18–20, 22, 25, 33, and 34.

Yahweh is using the possessive form to describe a **mountain** that belongs to the tribe of **Ephraim**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [on the mountain that belongs to Ephraim]

6.q: קָרְא֥וּ נֹצְרִ֖ים בְּ⁠הַ֣ר אֶפְרָ֑יִם ק֚וּמוּ וְ⁠נַעֲלֶ֣ה צִיּ֔וֹן
6.note: Yahweh is quoting the words that the watchers will call out. Consider natural ways of introducing direct quotations in your language. Alternate translation: [the watchers on the mountain of Ephraim will call out, saying, ‘Arise, and let us go up to Zion]
See how you translated this phrase in 26:13. This also occurs in verse 18.

7.note: See how you translated the similar expression in 24:8.

Yahweh is using this possessive form to mean the nation that is foremost among all **the nations**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [for the nation that is foremost among all nations]

Yahweh is using this possessive form to mean the part of **Israel** that is still alive. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the Israelites who still survive]

8.note: **Behold me** is an expression that people of this culture would commonly use to mean that they were about to do something. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Now I am about to bring them]
See how you translated the similar expression in 6:22.
See how you translated the similar expression in 6:22.

Yahweh is using the adjectives **the blind** and **the lame** as nouns to mean certain kinds of people. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate these adjectives with equivalent phrases. Alternate translation: [are people who are blind and people who are lame]

9.note: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **mercy**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and as they beg me to be merciful to them I will lead them]

Yahweh is using the possessive form to describe **streams** that consist of flowing **water**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [streams of flowing water]

Here Yahweh is speaking of the way by which he will bring his people home as if it were **a straight road** that was level and free of obstacles. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [by an easy way]

The pronoun **it** refers to the **straight road** on which Yahweh will lead his people. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [they will not stumble on that road]

9.q: הָיִ֤יתִי לְ⁠יִשְׂרָאֵל֙ לְ⁠אָ֔ב וְ⁠אֶפְרַ֖יִם בְּכֹ֥רִ⁠י הֽוּא
9.note: Here Yahweh is speaking of himself as if he were **a father** and of the people of Israel as if they were his **firstborn** son. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I care for Israel as my own child, and Ephraim is especially precious to me]

The pronoun **he** refers to **Ephraim**, that is, to the tribe of Ephraim, which stands for the whole northern kingdom. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [and Ephraim, that tribe is my firstborn]

10.note: See how you translated the similar expression in 2:4.
Yahweh is quoting the words that the nations are to declare in the coastlands. Consider natural ways of introducing direct quotations in your language. See the UST.

The pronoun **he** refers to Yahweh, and the pronoun **him** refers to the people of Israel. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [will gather the people of Israel, and Yahweh will protect them]

The point of this comparison is that just as **a shepherd** watches over **his flock**, so Yahweh will watch over the people of Israel. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [he will watch over him carefully, just as a shepherd watches over his flock]

Yahweh is using the possessive form to describe a **shepherd** who owns and cares for a **flock**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [like a shepherd who owns the flock]

11.note: See how you translated the similar expression in 10:25.

The pronouns **him** and **he** both refer to **Jacob**, that is, to the people of Israel. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [redeemed the Israelites from the hand of someone stronger than the Israelites]

Here, **the hand** represents the power and control of a person. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [from the control of one stronger than he]

12.note: The word **And** indicates that the events it introduces will take place after the events that Yahweh has just described. Your language may have a connecting word or phrase that you can use to show this. Alternate translation: [Afterward they will come and will sing on the height of Zion]

Yahweh is using this possessive form to mean the high place that is **Zion**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [on the high place of Zion] or [on the top of Mount Zion]

Here Yahweh is speaking of the joy that his people will feel as if it would make them **radiant** with light. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and they will be full of joy because of the goodness of Yahweh]

Yahweh is using this possessive form to mean the good things that **Yahweh** gives to his people. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the good things that Yahweh gives them]

Yahweh is using the possessive form to describe **the young** animals that belong to **the flock and the herd**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the young animals born to the flocks and the herds]

The pronoun **their** refers to the people of Israel whom Yahweh will bring back to Zion. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [And the soul of those people will be like a watered garden]

The point of this comparison is that just as **a watered garden** is fresh and flourishing, so the people of Israel will thrive. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [And they will flourish like a well-watered garden]

13.note: The word **Then** indicates that the events it introduces will take place after the events that Yahweh has just described. Your language may have a connecting word or phrase that you can use to show this. Alternate translation: [After that,]

Yahweh is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and the young men and the old will rejoice with dancing together]

Yahweh is using the adjective **the old** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [and the old people]

Here Yahweh is speaking as if **mourning** were an object that he could **turn** into something else. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And I will cause them to be joyful instead of mournful]

These two clauses mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Another approach would be to connect the phrases with a word that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. See how you as a team have decided to translate the parallel phrases in poetry, and follow that approach here and throughout this chapter. Alternate translation: [And I will turn their mourning to joy, causing them to rejoice rather than be sorrowful]

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **mourning** and **joy**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [And I will cause them to stop mourning and to rejoice instead]

14.note: Here Yahweh is speaking of the abundant provision that he will give to the priests as if it were **fatness** with which he would soak them. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I will abundantly provide for the priests]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **fatness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [saturate the soul of the priests with rich food]

Yahweh is using the possessive form to describe the inner being that belongs to **the priests**, that is, the priests themselves. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the priests themselves]

The expression **will be satisfied** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [my goodness will satisfy my people]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **goodness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [satisfied with how good I am to them]

15.note: The expression **is heard** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [People hear a voice in Ramah]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **bitterness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [bitter weeping]

Yahweh is speaking of **Rachel**, an ancestor of the people of Israel who had died long before this, as if she were alive and weeping over her descendants. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Every mother in Israel is weeping over her sons]

The expression **to be comforted** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [she refuses to let anyone comfort her]
The pronoun **he** refers to **her sons**, whom Yahweh speaks of here as a single group. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [for her sons are gone]
See how you translated the similar expression in 10:20.

16.note: Here, **your voice** and **your eyes** represent the act of weeping. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [Stop weeping and stop shedding tears]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **work**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [I will reward you for what you have done]
The pronoun **they** refers to the children of the people whom Yahweh is addressing here. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [and your children will return]

Yahweh is using the possessive form to describe a **land** that belongs to **the enemy**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [from the land that belongs to the enemy]

17.note: If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **hope** and **future**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [And you can confidently expect what will happen later]

If it would be more natural in your language, you may want to put the information about the **sons** who will return before the information about their returning. Alternate translation: [and your sons will return to their border]

18.note: Yahweh is using a construction in which a verb and a related form come from the same root. You may be able to use the same construction in your language to express the meaning here. Alternatively, your language may have another way of saying this. Alternate translation: [I have indeed heard Ephraim]
Yahweh is using the name **Ephraim**, one of the tribes, to represent all of the people of Israel, the northern kingdom. Alternate translation: [people of Israel]
Yahweh is quoting the words that the people of Ephraim say as they grieve. Consider natural ways of introducing direct quotations in your language.

The point of this comparison is that just as **a calf not trained** resists the yoke that its owner puts on it, so the people of Ephraim resisted the discipline that Yahweh gave them. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [and I resisted your discipline, just as an untrained calf resists the yoke]

The expression **I was disciplined** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and you disciplined me like someone disciplines a calf that no one has trained]

The expression **not trained** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [like a calf that no one has trained]

Here the people of Ephraim are speaking of repenting and being restored to Yahweh as if it were a physical **return** to a place. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Cause me to repent, and I will repent]

The people of Ephraim are using this possessive form to describe their relationship with **Yahweh** as the God whom they worship and to whom they belong. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [you are Yahweh, the God whom I worship]

19.note: The word **after** indicates that the event it introduces took place following the event that the people of Ephraim have just mentioned. Your language may have a connecting word or phrase that you can use to show this. Alternate translation: [For I turned away, and then I repented, and after that I was made to know]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **turning away**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [after I turned away, I repented]

The expression **my being made to know** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and after you made me know my sin]

The people of Ephraim is using **I struck on my thigh** as a common expression of the culture to mean “I showed that I was deeply grieved and ashamed.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I showed my deep grief]

The expressions **I was ashamed** and **I was humiliated** mean similar things. The people of Ephraim are using the two expressions together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [I was deeply ashamed]

The expressions **I was ashamed** and **I was humiliated** are passive verbal forms. If it would be unnatural to use those forms, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [I felt ashamed and also disgraced]

The people of Ephraim are using this possessive form to mean the disgrace that they brought on themselves during their **youth**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the disgrace that I brought on myself when I was young]

20.q: הֲ⁠בֵן֩ יַקִּ֨יר לִ֜⁠י אֶפְרַ֗יִם אִ֚ם יֶ֣לֶד שַׁעֲשֻׁעִ֔ים
20.note: Yahweh is using the question form to express his deep affection for the people of Ephraim. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [Ephraim is indeed a precious son to me, a child in whom I delight!]

The pronoun **him** refers to Ephraim, that is, to the people of the northern kingdom of Israel. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [as often as I speak against the people of Ephraim]

Yahweh is using a construction in which a verb and a related form come from the same root. You may be able to use the same construction in your language to express the meaning here. Alternatively, your language may have another way of saying this. See the UST.

Here, **my inward parts** represents the deepest feelings of a person. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [I deeply long for him]

Yahweh is using a construction in which a verb and a related form come from the same root. You may be able to use the same construction in your language to express the meaning here. Alternatively, your language may have another way of saying this. See the UST.

21.q: הַצִּ֧יבִי לָ֣⁠ךְ צִיֻּנִ֗ים שִׂ֤מִי לָ⁠ךְ֙ & תַּמְרוּרִ֔ים
21.note: These two clauses mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Another approach would be to connect the phrases with a word that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. See how you as a team have decided to translate the parallel phrases in poetry, and follow that approach here and throughout this chapter. Alternate translation: [Set up road signs for yourselves, indeed, put up markers for yourselves]

Here, **your heart** represents the attention and the thinking of a person. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [Pay careful attention to the highway] or [Focus on the highway]

The pronoun **you** refers to the people of Israel, whom Yahweh addresses here as the **virgin of Israel**. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the road you Israelites walked]

Here Yahweh is speaking of the people of Israel as if they were a young woman, a **virgin**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Return, pure young nation of Israel]

22.note: Yahweh is using the question form to rebuke his people for their unfaithfulness to him. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [You have wavered long enough, apostate daughter!]

Here Yahweh is speaking of the people of Israel as if they were an unfaithful **daughter**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [unfaithful people]

Yahweh is using **a female will surround a man protectively** as a common expression of the culture to mean “the weak will guard the strong.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the weak will guard the strong]

23.q: ע֣וֹד יֹאמְר֞וּ אֶת־הַ⁠דָּבָ֣ר הַ⁠זֶּ֗ה בְּ⁠אֶ֤רֶץ יְהוּדָה֙ וּ⁠בְ⁠עָרָ֔י⁠ו בְּ⁠שׁוּבִ֖⁠י אֶת־שְׁבוּתָ֑⁠ם
23.note: The word that the ULT translates as **when** indicates that the people will say these words at the same time that Yahweh restores their fortune. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could describe the time relationship more explicitly. Alternate translation: [During the time that I return their restoration, they will again say this word in the land of Judah and in its cities]
See how you translated the similar expression in 29:14.
Yahweh is quoting the words that the people of Judah will say. Consider natural ways of introducing direct quotations in your language. See the UST.

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **righteousness** and **holiness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [dwelling place of Yahweh who is righteous, on the mountain that is set apart to him]

24.note: The pronoun **it** refers to the land of Judah, which Yahweh mentioned in the previous verse. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [And in that land Judah and all its cities will dwell together]
See how you translated the similar expression in 19:15.

25.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you may want to put the information about what Yahweh **will fill** before the information about **every languishing soul** that he will fill. Alternate translation: [I will fill every languishing soul]

26.note: Jeremiah is using the phrase translated as **At this** to introduce a new event in the story. Use a word, phrase, or other method in your language that is natural for introducing a new event.

The pronoun **I** refers to Jeremiah, not to Yahweh, who had been speaking in the previous verses. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [At this I, Jeremiah, awoke and looked]

Jeremiah is using the possessive form to describe **sleep** that he himself experienced. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and the sleep that I had slept was pleasant to me]

27.note: Yahweh is using the term **Behold** to focus the listeners’ attention on what he is about to say. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [Pay attention, for the time is coming]
See how you translated the similar expression in 7:32.

The word **when** indicates that the events it introduces will take place after the time when Jeremiah was speaking. Your language may have a connecting word or phrase that you can use to show this. Alternate translation: [and then I will sow]

27.q: וְ⁠זָרַעְתִּ֗י אֶת־בֵּ֤ית יִשְׂרָאֵל֙ וְ⁠אֶת־בֵּ֣ית יְהוּדָ֔ה זֶ֥רַע אָדָ֖ם וְ⁠זֶ֥רַע בְּהֵמָֽה
27.note: Here Yahweh is speaking of greatly increasing the number of people and animals in the land as if he would **sow** the land with **seed**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [when I will cause the people and the animals of the house of Israel and the house of Judah to become numerous]

Here, **house** means all the people descended from a particular person. It envisions them as if they were one household living together. So **the house of Judah** figuratively means all the people descended from Judah. Alternate translation: [the people of Israel and the people of Judah]

Yahweh is using this possessive form to mean the offspring that **man** and **beast** produce. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [with offspring that people produce and offspring that animals produce]
See how you translated “seed” in 7:15 where it is used with the same meaning. Alternate translation: [with the offspring of people and the offspring of animals]

28.q: וְ⁠הָיָ֞ה כַּ⁠אֲשֶׁ֧ר שָׁקַ֣דְתִּי עֲלֵי⁠הֶ֗ם לִ⁠נְת֧וֹשׁ וְ⁠לִ⁠נְת֛וֹץ וְ⁠לַ⁠הֲרֹ֖ס וּ⁠לְ⁠הַאֲבִ֣יד וּ⁠לְ⁠הָרֵ֑עַ כֵּ֣ן אֶשְׁקֹ֧ד עֲלֵי⁠הֶ֛ם לִ⁠בְנ֥וֹת וְ⁠לִ⁠נְט֖וֹעַ
28.note: Yahweh is using **just as I watched over them to uproot and to tear down, and to overthrow and to destroy and to bring harm** to describe something that he was doing over a period of time. This provides the background for what he goes on to say about what he will do soon. Connect this clause to what follows in a way that makes it clear in your language that this clause is describing something that was ongoing in the background. Alternate translation: [And it will happen that, just as I had been watching over them to uproot and to tear down, and to overthrow and to destroy and to bring harm, so I will watch over them to build and to plant]

The pronoun **them** refers to the people of Israel and Judah, whom Yahweh mentioned in the previous verse. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [just as I watched over the people of Israel and Judah]

28.q: שָׁקַ֣דְתִּי עֲלֵי⁠הֶ֗ם לִ⁠נְת֧וֹשׁ וְ⁠לִ⁠נְת֛וֹץ וְ⁠לַ⁠הֲרֹ֖ס וּ⁠לְ⁠הַאֲבִ֣יד
28.note: Here Yahweh is speaking of the way he judged his people as if he were a farmer who would **uproot** plants and a builder who would **tear down** structures. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I watched over them to remove them from their land and to demolish what they had built, and to defeat them and to ruin them]

Here Yahweh is speaking of restoring his people as if he were a builder who would **build** and a farmer who would **plant**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [thus I will watch over them to make them prosper again]
See how you translated the similar expression in 18:9.

29.note: The words that the ULT translates as **In those days** indicate that what follows will be true at the same time as the events that Yahweh has just described. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could describe the time relationship more explicitly. Alternate translation: [At the same time that I am rebuilding and replanting them]

The pronoun **they** refers to the people of Israel and Judah. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [In those days the people of Israel and Judah will no longer say]
Yahweh is quoting a proverb that the people had been saying. Consider natural ways of introducing direct quotations in your language.

29.q: אָב֖וֹת אָ֣כְלוּ בֹ֑סֶר וְ⁠שִׁנֵּ֥י בָנִ֖ים תִּקְהֶֽינָה
29.note: Here Yahweh quotes a proverb that the people used in order to complain that they were being punished for what their ancestors had done. Translate this proverb in a way that will be recognized as a proverb and be meaningful in your language and culture. Alternate translation: [The parents ate the sour fruit, but the children are the ones whose teeth are set on edge]

The people is using **the teeth of the children will become blunt** as a common expression of the culture to mean “the children suffer for what their parents did.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and the children are the ones punished for it]

The people were using the possessive form to describe **the teeth** that belong to **the children**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and the children are the ones whose teeth]

30.note: Yahweh uses the word **But** here to indicate a contrast between the proverb that the people had been saying and what will actually be true. In your translation, indicate this contrast in a way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [But instead,]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **iniquity**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [will die because he himself acted wickedly]

Here Yahweh is speaking of a person who sins as if he were a person who **eats the sour grapes**, and of the punishment for that sin as if it were the effect on that person’s own **teeth**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [every man who sins, he himself will suffer the punishment]

31.note: Yahweh is using the term **Behold** to focus the listeners’ attention on what he is about to say. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [Pay attention]

31.q: וְ⁠כָרַתִּ֗י אֶת־בֵּ֧ית יִשְׂרָאֵ֛ל וְ⁠אֶת־בֵּ֥ית יְהוּדָ֖ה בְּרִ֥ית חֲדָשָֽׁה
31.note: Yahweh is using **cut a…covenant** as a common expression of the culture to mean “make a covenant.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [when I will establish a new covenant]

32.note: Yahweh uses the words **It will not be like** here to indicate a contrast between the new covenant that Yahweh will make and the covenant that he made with the ancestors of the people. In your translation, indicate this contrast in a way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [It will be unlike the covenant that I cut with their fathers]

Yahweh is using **the covenant that I cut** as a common expression of the culture to mean “the covenant that I made.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. 32.q: בְּ⁠יוֹם֙ הֶחֱזִיקִ֣⁠י בְ⁠יָדָ֔⁠ם לְ⁠הוֹצִיאָ֖⁠ם מֵ⁠אֶ֖רֶץ מִצְרָ֑יִם
32.note: The words that the ULT translates as **on the day** indicate that Yahweh made that covenant at the same time as he brought the people out of Egypt. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could describe the time relationship more explicitly. Alternate translation: [at the time when I took hold of their hand to bring them out from the land of Egypt]

Here, **their hand** represents the people themselves as Yahweh led them. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [my taking hold of them]

Yahweh is stating the pronoun **they** separately, even though the verb translated as **they broke** already includes this meaning. He is doing that to emphasize that it was not Yahweh but the people who broke the covenant. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [which the Israelite people broke]

Yahweh uses the word **although** here to indicate a contrast between the way the people treated the covenant and the way Yahweh treated the people. In your translation, indicate this contrast in a way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [even though I was a husband to them]

Here Yahweh is speaking of his relationship with the people of Israel as if he were **a husband** and they were his wife. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [although I was faithfully committed to them]

33.note: Yahweh is using this possessive form to mean the people who are descended from **Israel**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [with the Israelites]

Here Yahweh is speaking of causing his people to know and desire his law as if he would put it inside their bodies and **write** it on their **heart**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I will cause them to know my law, and I will make them want to obey it]

Yahweh is using the possessive form to describe a **law** that comes from him. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [I will put the law that I have given in their inward parts]

34.note: The term translated as **And** indicates that what follows is a result of what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes this clear. Alternate translation: [This is why]

Here the masculine term **a man** has a generic sense that includes both men and women. 34.q: וְ⁠לֹ֧א יְלַמְּד֣וּ ע֗וֹד אִ֣ישׁ אֶת־רֵעֵ֜⁠הוּ וְ⁠אִ֤ישׁ אֶת־אָחִי⁠ו֙
34.note: Yahweh is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [will a man teach his neighbor and a man teach his brother]
Yahweh is quoting the words that people would say when they taught one another. Consider natural ways of introducing direct quotations in your language.

Yahweh is referring to all of the people by naming two extremes, **the smallest of them** and **the greatest of them**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [every last one of them]

Here Yahweh is speaking of choosing not to punish his people for their sin as if he would no longer **remember** it. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I will forgive their iniquity, and I will no longer punish them for their sin]

If it would be more natural in your language, you may want to put the information about **its waves** together with the information about the **sea** that Yahweh stirs up. Alternate translation: [the one stirring up the waves of the sea so that they roar]

Here, **his name** represents Yahweh himself and his reputation. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [He is known as Yahweh of Armies]

36.note: Yahweh is presenting a possible condition, that the fixed order that he has established for the sun, the moon, and the stars would come to an end. Use a natural form in your language for introducing a condition that could happen. Alternate translation: [If these statutes should ever depart from before me]

Yahweh is using **all the days** as a common expression of the culture to mean “forever” or “for as long as time continues.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [as long as days continue] or [forever]

37.q: אִם־יִמַּ֤דּוּ שָׁמַ֨יִם֙ מִ⁠לְ⁠מַ֔עְלָ⁠ה וְ⁠יֵחָקְר֥וּ מֽוֹסְדֵי־אֶ֖רֶץ לְ⁠מָ֑טָּה

37.q: אִם־יִמַּ֤דּוּ שָׁמַ֨יִם֙ מִ⁠לְ⁠מַ֔עְלָ⁠ה וְ⁠יֵחָקְר֥וּ מֽוֹסְדֵי־אֶ֖רֶץ לְ⁠מָ֑טָּה

If it would be unnatural to use those forms, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [If anyone can measure the heavens above and search out the foundations of the earth below]

Yahweh is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and if the foundations of the earth below can be measured and searched out]

Yahweh is presenting a possible condition, that someone would be able to measure the heavens and search out the foundations of the earth. Use a natural form in your language for introducing a condition that could happen. Alternate translation: [Suppose the heavens above can be measured]

Yahweh is using this possessive form to mean the **foundations** on which **the earth** rests. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the base that supports the earth below]

Yahweh is stating the pronoun **I** separately, even though the verb translated as **I will reject** already includes this meaning. 39.q: וְ⁠יָצָ֨א ע֜וֹד קוה הַ⁠מִּדָּה֙ נֶגְדּ֔⁠וֹ עַ֖ל גִּבְעַ֣ת גָּרֵ֑ב

The words **Kidron** and **the Gate of the Horses** are the names of places in and near the city of Jerusalem.
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **holiness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [will be set apart for Yahweh]

Here Yahweh is speaking of the destruction of the city as if the city were a plant that could be **uprooted**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [It will never be destroyed, and it will not be overthrown again forever]

The expressions **be uprooted** and **be overthrown** are passive verbal forms. If it would be unnatural to use those forms, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [No one will ever uproot it or overthrow it again]

The pronoun **It** refers twice to the city of Jerusalem. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [The city of Jerusalem will not be uprooted or overthrown again forever]

If it would be clearer in your language, you could use a positive expression to translate this. Alternate translation: [it will remain forever]
